title: Meet Sarah, My New Virtual Assistant
author: Michael G. Wagner
summary: Michael Wagner describes setting up an always-on autonomous AI assistant, an instance of Meta's Muse that he named Sarah, to manage his personal email, calendar and content ideas. The practical account is a vehicle for his real concern as a university educator: such an agent can log into any system its owner can, and do so with the owner's credentials. He tested this in a Canvas shell during a term with no student data and saw that the agent could run a whole course, from posting assignments to grading, without the system being able to tell it was not him. The same capability is available to any student, who could have an assistant read modules, post to forums, take quizzes and submit essays, which undermines the assumption that whoever logs in is doing the work. He is not alarmed by the possibility but by how few educators know about it, so he urges AI literacy, hands-on experimentation with personal accounts only, and strict separation from institutional logins and student data.
points: Always-on agents such as Muse, GrokBot and OpenAI's Dots can act with the user's full credentials, so anything a person can do online the agent can do autonomously.
Wagner keeps his assistant away from work email because student grade communication is protected data that would otherwise leave the institution for a vendor's systems.
His Canvas test showed an agent could create, post, discuss and grade an entire course with no way for the platform to distinguish it from the instructor.
The same setup lets a student's assistant complete a course from the other side, which breaks the premise of much online teaching that the logged-in person is the one doing the work.
His recommended response is AI literacy: experiment on a personal account, keep student data out of reach, maintain backups, and redesign courses rather than hope students will not try it.
quotes: Sarah has her own browser and can log into any system I can log into, and once she is in, she has access to everything I have access to.

Most importantly, Sarah could log into Canvas and run all my courses on her own. She could create assignments, post them, talk to my students, review discussion forums, and step in wherever necessary.
And because she would be acting with my credentials, the system would have no way of knowing it was not me.

The problem is that everything I just described works for students, too. Any student can spin up a virtual assistant, whether through GrokBot, Muse, Dots, or whatever comes next, and give it access to their Canvas account.
And because she would be logging in with the student’s credentials, the teacher would have no way of knowing who actually did the work.
If you think about it, a lot of online teaching rests on the idea that whoever logs in is the person doing the work. That idea no longer holds.

What frightens me instead is that the vast majority of educators do not have the slightest idea that the latest advances in AI are pulling the rug out from under their feet. We therefore desperately need more AI literacy among educators.
Use a personal email account, keep the assistant far away from your institutional logins and anything involving student data, and make sure your backups are in order.
